synopsis: A journey through the vast, diffuse dust tail of Halley's Comet, with the distant sun shining through.

shots.prompt:
One continuous 15-second first-person flight at 24 fps, filmed as if the camera itself is the spacecraft, moving forward without pause for the entire take. Seconds 0-4 are calm and wide: the real body fills one side of the frame, lit hard from the side, the far sun flaring at the frame edge, and the camera is already drifting forward. Seconds 4-6 accelerate toward the obstacle field and the first objects slide into frame. Seconds 6-13 race through the field itself: objects rush past on both sides and overhead, the nearest ones blurring, fine particles streaking past the lens, objects colliding and bursting apart, the body still showing through the gaps. Seconds 13-15 plunge into the densest part and the frame fills with the climax, the brightest and most overwhelming moment of the whole take, still moving forward as it ends. One continuous take, no cut, no fade, no scene change, and the camera never stops or hovers. Nothing of the vehicle is visible: no cockpit, no hull, no instruments, no HUD. No text, no captions, no logos, no watermark, no people. Sound: diegetic only and locked to what is on screen, a deep low rumble running under the whole flight, quiet and distant at the start, sharp impacts hitting exactly when objects collide, the whole sound field growing continuously and reaching its loudest and fullest in the final two seconds. No music, no voice, no narration.

A flight through the diffuse, golden dust tail of Halley's Comet. The comet's dark, irregular nucleus is a hazy outline in the far distance, partially obscured by its own emissions. The sun flares brightly at the top left edge of the frame. At 0-4 seconds, the camera drifts calmly through the outer reaches of the tail. The view is wide, showing the faint, shimmering glow of the dust tail extending infinitely. A low, distant hum accompanies the serene flight. From 4-6 seconds, acceleration begins, pulling the camera deeper into the tail. Sparse, tiny dust grains, appearing as faint specks of light, begin to drift into view from the sides, hinting at the increasing density ahead. Between 6-13 seconds, the flight races through the main body of the dust tail. Billions of micro-sized dust particles stream past the lens, creating a sense of immense speed and motion blur on the nearest objects. Occasional larger, pebble-sized ice and rock fragments, glinting in the distant sunlight, tumble past, sometimes colliding with a faint, sharp 'ping' sound. The comet nucleus remains a slightly more defined, dark shape in the background, surrounded by a faint coma. From 13-15 seconds, the camera plunges into a particularly dense stream of dust particles, closest to the nucleus. The entire frame fills with a torrent of fast-streaking, brightly lit dust, creating a overwhelming sense of speed and immersion. The sound escalates to a full, continuous roar of rushing particles, punctuated by rapid-fire impacts, ending as the view is completely consumed by the glittering dust storm.

caption:
This flight takes us through the dusty tail of Halley's Comet, a famous short-period comet that visits every 75-76 years.

The obstacle field comprises trillions of silicate dust grains and ice particles, typically micrometers to millimeters in size, shed from the comet's nucleus and pushed away by solar radiation pressure. These particles can be separated by tens to hundreds of kilometers.

Halley's Comet was famously observed by the European Space Agency's Giotto probe in 1986, which flew within 600 kilometers of its nucleus, capturing images and analyzing the dust and gas in its coma and tail.

Flying through the dust tail is impossible for a spacecraft due to the high relative velocity, which turns even microscopic dust grains into hypervelocity projectiles. These impacts would rapidly abrade the spacecraft, puncturing vital systems and rendering it inoperable.

This is a simulation, not real footage. What do you think is the biggest difference between the dust tail and the ion tail?
